issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a civilian in a war zone, broad self-blame for the event is hard to reconcile unless there are other items indicating a specific morally injurious or preventable action. The rest of the profile centers on external danger cues (being followed/watched, loud sounds, checking safety) and vulnerability, not guilt-linked processing. This appraisal is therefore the main clinically questionable item in the set.

vignette:
Layla Mansour is a forty-four-year-old married woman of Lebanese origin who works as a prosecutor in a mid-sized American city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that she had, until recently, managed to conceal behind the disciplined composure her courtroom career demanded. Her presenting difficulties trace back to a period approximately three years ago when she returned to Beirut to care for her elderly mother during a stretch of renewed urban conflict. What she encountered there - the sudden percussion of shelling, the nights spent in a basement corridor listening to boots moving on the street above, the sensation of being tracked through a neighbourhood that had become a grid of checkpoints and watchful strangers - left marks she did not immediately recognise as injury.

During those weeks in Beirut, Layla had learned to read sound as information about survival. A voice carrying through a stairwell, the cadence of footsteps behind her on a narrow street, the feeling that someone at a checkpoint was following her progress with more than routine interest - each of these had, at one point or another, preceded a moment of genuine danger. She returned to the United States believing she had simply endured something difficult and moved on. It took months before she noticed that the learning had not reversed.

The triggers that now govern her daily life are precisely those that were forged in Beirut. When a male voice in an adjacent office rises unexpectedly, or carries a particular gravel quality she cannot fully articulate, Layla's body responds before her mind catches up. The sensation of being followed - which she encounters almost daily during the walk from the parking structure to the courthouse - arrives without warning and feels entirely credible, even when she can see with her own eyes that the street is ordinary. The feeling of being watched is perhaps the most disruptive, because the courtroom is, by design, a place where she is observed. When these triggers fire, they do not stay contained. They open immediately into a state of threat that reorganises her entire attention: she wakes during the night to check the locks and listen at the bedroom door, she has identified only her home office and one corner of her living room as places where she can breathe without scanning, and she remains on high alert whenever an unexpected sound - a door slamming in the courthouse corridor, a car backfiring outside - reaches her before she has had time to prepare for it. The trigger and the threat response have become so tightly coupled that each feeds the other: the hypervigilant scanning she maintains throughout the day makes her more likely to register ambiguous stimuli as threatening, which in turn produces new surges of alarm that confirm, to her, that the scanning is necessary.

This sustained state of threat has quietly eroded the way Layla understands herself and the world she inhabits. She had come to believe, with a flatness that frightened her more than the fear itself, that the person she used to be - someone her husband described as warm, even buoyant - was simply gone. She was certain that she could no longer manage the ordinary friction of life; a minor scheduling conflict at work, a raised voice in a meeting, a small domestic disagreement with her husband would leave her undone in ways that felt humiliating for a woman who prosecuted violent felonies without flinching. And undergirding all of it was a conviction, now almost axiomatic, that the world is a place where danger is the baseline condition and safety is always provisional. The heightened threat monitoring that had begun as a response to specific triggers had, over time, supplied her with daily evidence for this belief, making it feel not like a symptom but like accurate perception.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was a morning in the courthouse when she stepped into an elevator, heard a man behind her speaking in Arabic on his phone, and had to exit before the doors closed. She stood in the lobby, professionally dressed and entirely unable to re-enter the building for eleven minutes. She told no one. But that evening she made the referral call herself, and what she said she most wanted - quietly, without much hope - was to be able to do her job without being afraid of a voice in a hallway.
